learn.title: Measuring work
learn.body: Seconds are a poor measure of an algorithm. A fast phone and an old laptop give different times. Instead we count steps, such as comparisons or additions, as a function of the input size $n$. That count is the same on any machine.

learn.title: Counting a simple loop
learn.body: This loop adds the numbers 1 to `n`. Its body runs once per number, so it does $n$ additions.

learn.title: What to count
learn.body: With n = 10 the loop makes 10 additions and prints 55. With n = 100 it makes 100 additions. The work grows in step with n. We choose one kind of step, usually the most repeated one, and count how many times it runs.

learn.title: A loop inside a loop
learn.body: For each `i`, the inner loop runs `n` times. So the body runs $n \cdot n$ times.

learn.title: How the count grows
learn.body: Compare the two loops as n gets bigger.
steps: For the single loop, n = 10 gives 10 steps
For the double loop, n = 10 gives 100 steps
Double the input to n = 20: the single loop does 20, the double loop does 400
Doubling n doubles one count but quadruples the other

learn.body: Count the work inside the loops, not the lines of code. A short nested loop can cost far more than a long loop with no nesting.

questions.prompt: Why do we count steps instead of timing a program?
choices: Counting does not depend on the machine
Counting is always exact in seconds
Timers do not work in C
questions.explanation: The step count is a property of the algorithm. Time also depends on the computer.

questions.prompt: How many times does `total += i;` run when `n` is 10?
questions.explanation: The loop goes from `i = 1` to `i = 10`, so the body runs 10 times.

questions.prompt: How many times does `count++` run in the double loop when `n` is 5?
questions.explanation: The outer loop runs 5 times and each time the inner loop runs 5 times: 5 times 5 is 25.

questions.prompt: In the double loop, `n` goes from 10 to 20. By what factor does the work grow?
questions.explanation: 100 steps become 400 steps. Squaring the size means doubling n multiplies the work by 4.

questions.prompt: We measure how the number of steps grows as the input size \_\_ grows.
questions.explanation: The letter n stands for the input size, for example the length of an array.

questions.prompt: Match each loop to the number of times its body runs.
pairs: loop that runs 3 times, nested in a loop of 4
questions.explanation: Nested loops multiply, and one loop adds up to its limit.

questions.prompt: A loop runs the body 1000 times for n = 1000. What is the most likely step count for n = 2000?
questions.explanation: The count grows in step with n, so it doubles.
